subject: Coffee & Tea
title: Withdrawal Symptoms
description: A micro-lesson that makes Withdrawal Symptoms usable.

hook.text: Stop drinking coffee suddenly and within 12–24 hours, you may get a splitting headache. That's withdrawal.

buildup.text: Caffeine constricts brain blood vessels. Without it, vessels dilate, causing the classic throbbing caffeine headache.

discovery.text: Other symptoms include fatigue, irritability, difficulty concentrating, and even flu-like muscle aches.

twist.text: Withdrawal is now an official medical diagnosis—'caffeine withdrawal' appears in the DSM-5 (psychiatry's manual).

climax.text: Symptoms peak at 1–2 days and resolve within a week. Tapering gradually reduces or eliminates them entirely.

punchline.text: Your brain adapted to caffeine. Removing it hurts—temporarily.

quiz.question: What causes the classic caffeine withdrawal headache?
options: Brain blood vessels dilating when caffeine's constricting effect stops

details.summary: Caffeine withdrawal begins 12 to 24 hours after the last dose and peaks at one to two days. Symptoms include headache, fatigue, irritability, difficulty concentrating, and depressed mood. They typically resolve within a week as the brain's excess adenosine receptors normalize.
details.whyItMatters: Withdrawal symptoms are real and can be debilitating enough to affect work and daily function. Knowing the timeline helps people manage a deliberate reduction.
takeaways: Withdrawal starts 12 to 24 hours after the last caffeine dose
Headache and fatigue are the most commonly reported symptoms
Most symptoms resolve within five to nine days

faq.question: What is the best way to reduce caffeine intake without severe withdrawal?
faq.answer: Gradually reduce intake by about 25 percent every two to three days. This gives the brain time to downregulate extra adenosine receptors without triggering the full intensity of withdrawal symptoms.

faq.question: Why does caffeine withdrawal cause such intense headaches?
faq.answer: Caffeine constricts blood vessels in the brain. When you stop consuming it, those vessels suddenly dilate, increasing blood flow and pressure. This rebound vasodilation is the primary cause of withdrawal headaches.
